Per-cell QC metrics and outlier flagging

Source: vignettes/qcMetrics.Rmd
qcMetrics.Rmd
library(rscprep)

Two functions, in order. diagnoseQC() calculates the per-cell metrics that filtering decisions get made from; flagQC() marks the cells those metrics say are outliers. Neither one removes anything – the split is deliberate, so that you can look at what a threshold would cut before you cut it.

The example data

Every example in this vignette runs on data bundled with rscprep: a cut-down copy of the 10x Genomics demo run 1k Heart Cells from an E18 Mouse (v3 chemistry). It is one sample from one cellranger count run (Cell Ranger 3.0.0, mm10 reference), with all 1,011 cells Cell Ranger called.

It comes in two forms, holding the same data:

  • heart1k – a Seurat object, for examples that start after loading.
  • A Cell Ranger outs/ directory – for the functions that take a path. It holds filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5 (the called cells) and raw_feature_bc_matrix.h5 (every barcode that had at least 25 UMIs in the original run, empty droplets included):
outs <- system.file("extdata", "heart_1k_v3", "outs", package = "rscprep")

To keep the package small, only 2,092 of the 31,053 genes are kept: the 2,000 detected in the most cells, plus every mitochondrial, ribosomal protein and cell-cycle gene. Each cell therefore keeps about 70% of its UMIs, and percentages such as pctMito read higher than they would on the full gene set. That is fine for showing how the functions behave and wrong for drawing conclusions about heart tissue. ?heart1k has the details, and data-raw/heart_1k_v3.R in the package source rebuilds it from the 10x download.

Making several samples from one

heart1k is a single sample, and this vignette needs several. So the cells are dealt at random into three pseudo-samples, and two of them are thinned to look like shallower sequencing runs:

counts <- heart1k[["RNA"]]@counts

set.seed(1)
sample_of <- sample(c("Sample_A", "Sample_B", "Sample_C"), ncol(counts),
                    replace = TRUE)

# Fraction of each UMI count kept. Keeping each UMI with probability p
# ("binomial thinning") is what sequencing a library p times as deeply does.
depth <- c(Sample_A = 0.15, Sample_B = 0.4, Sample_C = 1)

seurat_list <- lapply(names(depth), function(s) {
  m    <- counts[, sample_of == s]
  m@x  <- as.numeric(stats::rbinom(length(m@x), m@x, depth[[s]]))
  m    <- Matrix::drop0(m)
  obj  <- Seurat::CreateSeuratObject(m, project = s,
                                     min.cells = 0, min.features = 0)
  obj$Ident <- s     # the sample-name column seuratFrom10x() would set
  obj
})
names(seurat_list) <- names(depth)

seurat_list
#> $Sample_A
#> An object of class Seurat 
#> 2092 features across 356 samples within 1 assay 
#> Active assay: RNA (2092 features, 0 variable features)
#>  1 layer present: counts
#> 
#> $Sample_B
#> An object of class Seurat 
#> 2092 features across 341 samples within 1 assay 
#> Active assay: RNA (2092 features, 0 variable features)
#>  1 layer present: counts
#> 
#> $Sample_C
#> An object of class Seurat 
#> 2092 features across 314 samples within 1 assay 
#> Active assay: RNA (2092 features, 0 variable features)
#>  1 layer present: counts

That list has the same shape seuratFrom10x() returns for a multi-sample run: named by sample, each object carrying its name in Ident. The cells are real, but the three “samples” are not separate biology. They differ only in simulated depth.

The three depths matter here: they are what the per-sample section below is about.

Where this starts

This vignette picks up where mergeSeurat() leaves off. With your own data that is:

seurat_list <- seuratFrom10x(manifest = manifest)
seurat_list <- includeMetadata(seurat_list, sample_sheet)
seurat      <- mergeSeurat(seurat_list)

Here it is the pseudo-sample list:

seurat <- mergeSeurat(seurat_list)
#> ℹ Merging 3 seurat objects...
#> ✔ Successfully merged 3 seurat objects.
tapply(seurat$nCount_RNA, seurat$Ident, median)
#> Sample_A Sample_B Sample_C 
#>      699     2343     5348

Both functions want that single merged object rather than the list, so that one set of thresholds is chosen from one view of the data.

Calculating the metrics 

seurat <- diagnoseQC(seurat, organism = "mmu")
#> ℹ Diagnosing 1011 cells in assay "RNA" using "mmu" gene patterns.
#> ℹ mito: 13 features matched "^mt".
#> ℹ ribo: 105 features matched "^Rp[sl]".
#> ✔ Added 3 QC metrics to 1011 cells.
#> • pctMito: median 9.95%, max 99.48%
#> • pctRibo: median 20.39%, max 56.36%
#> • log10GenesPerUMI: median 0.829

Three columns land in the metadata, alongside the nCount_RNA and nFeature_RNA that Seurat already wrote:

head(seurat@meta.data[, c("nCount_RNA", "nFeature_RNA",
                          "pctMito", "pctRibo", "log10GenesPerUMI")])
#>                             nCount_RNA nFeature_RNA   pctMito   pctRibo
#> Sample_A_AAACCCACACCAGTAT-1       1718          647  7.101281 31.490105
#> Sample_A_AAACCCAGTGGAACAC-1       1972          782  9.178499 23.326572
#> Sample_A_AAACGAAGTCAGGTGA-1        495           25  0.000000  4.040404
#> Sample_A_AACAACCAGGTTTGAA-1       1228          525 11.889251 35.016287
#> Sample_A_AACAAGATCGGATACT-1        916          428 36.899563  8.624454
#> Sample_A_AACAAGATCGGTAAGG-1       1654          684  8.464329 25.272068
#>                             log10GenesPerUMI
#> Sample_A_AAACCCACACCAGTAT-1        0.8688977
#> Sample_A_AAACCCAGTGGAACAC-1        0.8780845
#> Sample_A_AAACGAAGTCAGGTGA-1        0.5187921
#> Sample_A_AACAACCAGGTTTGAA-1        0.8805389
#> Sample_A_AACAAGATCGGATACT-1        0.8884324
#> Sample_A_AACAAGATCGGTAAGG-1        0.8808528
  • pctMito – share of a cell’s UMIs coming from mitochondrial genes. High means the cell lost cytoplasmic RNA through a ruptured membrane, so this is the usual first filter. What counts as high is tissue-dependent: 5–10% is a common starting point, but cardiac, muscle and kidney are legitimately mitochondria-rich and a fixed cutoff throws away real cells. This is heart: 50% of its cells are above 10%, and 30% above 20%. (The gene subset inflates these somewhat – see above.)
  • pctRibo – share from ribosomal protein genes. Rarely a hard filter, because it varies strongly by cell type. Useful as a comparison between samples that ought to look alike: a sharp shift points at something technical.
  • log10GenesPerUMI – library complexity, log10(nFeature) / log10(nCount). Between 0 and 1 for real cells; low means a library dominated by few transcripts. Around 0.8 is a conventional floor.

The percentages come from matching gene symbols against organism-specific patterns, so organism has to match the data.

When the patterns match nothing

Get the organism wrong and both columns come back as zeroes. That is loud rather than silent:

wrong <- diagnoseQC(seurat, organism = "hsa")   # mouse data
#> ℹ Diagnosing 1011 cells in assay "RNA" using "hsa" gene patterns.
#> Warning: ! mito pattern "^MT-" matched 0 features for organism "hsa".
#> ℹ Check that rownames are gene symbols and not Ensembl IDs --
#>   `head(rownames(seurat))` will show which.
#> ℹ pctMito will be 0 for every cell.
#> Warning: ! ribo pattern "^RP[SL]" matched 0 features for organism "hsa".
#> ℹ Check that rownames are gene symbols and not Ensembl IDs --
#>   `head(rownames(seurat))` will show which.
#> ℹ pctRibo will be 0 for every cell.
#> ✔ Added 3 QC metrics to 1011 cells.
#> • pctMito: median 0%, max 0%
#> • pctRibo: median 0%, max 0%
#> • log10GenesPerUMI: median 0.829

The same warning fires when the organism is right but the matrix is still keyed by Ensembl IDs, which is the other common cause – ENSMUSG00000064341 matches no symbol pattern. Convert the rownames to symbols before diagnosing.

Four organisms are supported, differing only in the capitalisation convention their symbols follow:

code organism mito ribo
"hsa" human ^MT- ^RP[SL]
"mmu" mouse ^mt ^Rp[sl]
"rno" rat ^Mt- ^Rp[sl]
"dre" zebrafish ^mt- ^rp[sl]

An organism not listed can borrow the code of one whose convention it shares.

Cell cycle, optionally

doCellCycle = TRUE also hands the object to runCellCycle(), adding S.Score, G2M.Score and Phase. It is not run here, because for mouse data it converts the human marker lists through orthogene, which needs network access:

seurat <- diagnoseQC(seurat, organism = "mmu", doCellCycle = TRUE)

It is off by default because, unlike the metrics above, scoring assumes normalised data – and will run Seurat::NormalizeData() on the object itself, with a warning, if it arrives raw. See ?runCellCycle for the detail, including the method argument for machines without network access.

Flagging outliers

flagQC() marks cells that sit an unusual distance from the rest, using the median absolute deviation rather than a fixed cutoff:

flagged <- flagQC(seurat, metrics = c(nFeature_RNA = "lower", pctMito = "higher"))
#> ℹ Flagging outliers in 2 metrics at 3 MADs from the median (log2 scale), across all cells.
#> ℹ nFeature_RNA: 14/1011 cells flagged (1.38%).
#> • lower: < 10.91 -- 14 cells
#> ℹ pctMito: 0/1011 cells flagged (0%).
#> • upper: > 167.5 -- 0 cells
#> ✔ Added 2 outlier columns; summary in `seurat@misc$flagQC`.

Each entry is column = bound, and the bound is per metric because which tail matters depends on the metric. nFeature_RNA wants "lower" – the low tail is empty droplets and dying cells, while the high tail is mostly real, well-captured cells. pctMito wants "higher", since high is bad and low is not. "both" is the default, and is what you want when doublets are the concern.

A MAD-based threshold adapts to the data, which a hard cutoff cannot: a cutoff carried between experiments discards good cells from a shallow run and keeps bad ones from a deep one. The cost is that it assumes most of the cells it is estimated from are good. On a badly failed sample it will call the failure normal and flag the survivors.

When the log scale is wrong

Look at the pctMito line above: an upper cutoff of 167%, which no cell can exceed. The MAD is estimated on a log2 scale by default. That suits count metrics, which are strongly right-skewed. But in this heart, pctMito runs from near 0 to 99%. On a log scale the cells near zero stretch the spread so far that 3 MADs above the median lands past 100%.

On the original scale the cutoff is usable:

flagged <- flagQC(flagged, metrics = c(pctMito = "higher"), log = FALSE)
#> ℹ Flagging outliers in 1 metric at 3 MADs from the median, across all cells.
#> ℹ pctMito: 149/1011 cells flagged (14.74%).
#> • upper: > 42.29 -- 149 cells
#> ✔ Added 2 outlier columns; summary in `flagged@misc$flagQC`.

Check the thresholds in the console output before you trust the flags. A cutoff outside the range a metric can take is the clearest sign the scale is wrong for it.

Estimating thresholds per sample

This is the argument that matters most. By default flagQC() estimates one threshold across every cell in the object. If your samples differ in sequencing depth – and they usually do – that single threshold describes none of them.

The three pseudo-samples have median depths of roughly 700, 2,340, and 5,350 UMIs. Globally:

global <- flagQC(seurat, c(nFeature_RNA = "lower"))
#> ℹ Flagging outliers in 1 metric at 3 MADs from the median (log2 scale), across all cells.
#> ℹ nFeature_RNA: 14/1011 cells flagged (1.38%).
#> • lower: < 10.91 -- 14 cells
#> ✔ Added 1 outlier column; summary in `seurat@misc$flagQC`.

table(global$Ident, flagged = global$nFeature_RNA_3_lower_outliers)
#>           flagged
#>            FALSE TRUE
#>   Sample_A   343   13
#>   Sample_B   340    1
#>   Sample_C   314    0

One cutoff, set mostly by the middle of the pooled data. It sits low for the deep sample and high for the shallow one, so its flags land on Sample_A because that sample was sequenced shallowly, not because its cells are worse. The deep sample’s poorest cells clear it easily.

Now per sample:

seurat <- flagQC(seurat, c(nFeature_RNA = "lower"), group_by = "Ident")
#> ℹ Flagging outliers in 1 metric at 3 MADs from the median (log2 scale), within 3 groups of Ident.
#> ℹ nFeature_RNA: 46/1011 cells flagged (4.55%) across 3 groups.
#> • lower: < 3.781-87.11 -- 46 cells
#> ✔ Added 1 outlier column; summary in `seurat@misc$flagQC`.

table(seurat$Ident, flagged = seurat$nFeature_RNA_3_lower_outliers)
#>           flagged
#>            FALSE TRUE
#>   Sample_A   353    3
#>   Sample_B   333    8
#>   Sample_C   279   35

Three thresholds instead of one, each set against its own sample’s distribution. The flags move to the cells that are poor for their sample, which in this case means mostly the deep one. The console prints the range across groups rather than a line per group, so a twenty-sample object stays readable; the per-group numbers are in the summary table below.

"Ident" is the sample name seuratFrom10x() sets, but any discrete metadata column works: a capture batch, a 10x lane, a tissue. Group on the technical variable you want the threshold to absorb.

pctMito is a ratio, so it does not scale with depth the way nFeature_RNA does, and depth is not a reason to group it. Flag it across all cells:

seurat <- flagQC(seurat, c(pctMito = "higher"), log = FALSE)
#> ℹ Flagging outliers in 1 metric at 3 MADs from the median, across all cells.
#> ℹ pctMito: 149/1011 cells flagged (14.74%).
#> • upper: > 42.29 -- 149 cells
#> ✔ Added 2 outlier columns; summary in `seurat@misc$flagQC`.

Reading the summary

Every call records what it did. getOutlierSummary() reads it back:

qc <- getOutlierSummary(seurat)
qc[, c("metric", "group", "lower", "upper", "n_flagged", "pct_flagged")]
#>         metric    group     lower    upper n_flagged pct_flagged
#> 1 nFeature_RNA Sample_A  3.780666       NA         3   0.8426966
#> 2 nFeature_RNA Sample_B 20.495647       NA         8   2.3460411
#> 3 nFeature_RNA Sample_C 87.106975       NA        35  11.1464968
#> 4      pctMito     <NA>        NA 42.29134       149  14.7378833

One row per metric per group. Two things to notice:

  • Thresholds are on the metric’s own scale, even though the nFeature_RNA estimate was made on a log scale. They can be compared against the column directly.
  • The unenforced tail is NA, not an unapplied number. nFeature_RNA was flagged "lower" only, so its upper is blank rather than a cutoff nothing was tested against. The same applies to n_lower / n_upper.

Which group is losing the most cells?

qc[order(-qc$pct_flagged), c("metric", "group", "n_flagged", "pct_flagged")]
#>         metric    group n_flagged pct_flagged
#> 4      pctMito     <NA>       149  14.7378833
#> 3 nFeature_RNA Sample_C        35  11.1464968
#> 2 nFeature_RNA Sample_B         8   2.3460411
#> 1 nFeature_RNA Sample_A         3   0.8426966

The two calls above accumulated into this one table: nFeature_RNA per sample, then pctMito across all cells. It is a record written at flag time, not a live view – cell counts describe the object as it stood then, which is the point, since being able to say afterwards how many cells were dropped and why is the reason to keep it.

Groups too small to estimate from

Per-group estimation creates a failure mode global estimation does not have. A group of two cells has no usable spread, and a group where over half the cells share one value has a MAD of zero. Both are skipped rather than given a meaningless threshold. Here, a made-up Lane column puts two cells in a lane of their own:

lanes <- seurat
lanes$Lane <- ifelse(seq_len(ncol(lanes)) <= 2, "Lane_3",
                     rep(c("Lane_1", "Lane_2"), length.out = ncol(lanes)))

lanes <- flagQC(lanes, c(nCount_RNA = "lower"), group_by = "Lane")
#> ℹ Flagging outliers in 1 metric at 3 MADs from the median (log2 scale), within 3 groups of Lane.
#> Warning: ! nCount_RNA: no threshold for 1 of 3 Lane groups.
#> ℹ Skipped: Lane_3 (fewer than 3 cells)
#> ✖ Cells in that group are left as NA, not FALSE.
#> ℹ nCount_RNA: 0/1009 cells flagged (0%) across 2 groups.
#> • lower: < 16.33-18.42 -- 0 cells
#> ✔ Added 3 outlier columns; summary in `lanes@misc$flagQC`.

One warning naming every skipped group, not one per group. Skipped groups still get a row in the summary table, with NA thresholds and an NA column, so nothing silently disappears.

That NA-not-FALSE distinction runs throughout. A cell is left NA when it was never judged – missing metric, missing group_by value, or a skipped group – so an unjudged cell is never mistaken for one that passed. It matters at the filtering step below.

Actually filtering

flagQC() writes logical columns and stops. Filtering is yours:

flags <- grep("_outliers$", colnames(seurat@meta.data), value = TRUE)
flags
#> [1] "nFeature_RNA_3_lower_outliers" "pctMito_3_higher_outliers"

# `%in% TRUE` treats an unjudged NA as "not an outlier"; use `isTRUE`-style
# logic deliberately rather than letting NA propagate through `|`
keep     <- !Reduce(`|`, lapply(seurat@meta.data[flags], function(x) x %in% TRUE))
filtered <- seurat[, which(keep)]

table(seurat$Ident, keep)
#>           keep
#>            FALSE TRUE
#>   Sample_A    58  298
#>   Sample_B    59  282
#>   Sample_C    74  240

Cross-tabulate before you subset. A sample losing far more than its neighbours is worth understanding rather than filtering: it may have failed, or it may be a genuinely different tissue where the thresholds do not transfer.

You do not have to trust every flag. The columns are independent, so filter on the subset you believe:

filtered <- seurat[, which(!seurat$pctMito_3_higher_outliers %in% TRUE)]
ncol(filtered)
#> [1] 862

Tuning 

# more aggressive
seurat <- flagQC(seurat, c(pctMito = "higher"), nmads = 2.5, log = FALSE)

# keep all but the extremes
seurat <- flagQC(seurat, c(pctMito = "higher"), nmads = 5, log = FALSE)

# a metric that is already symmetric does not want the log transform
seurat <- flagQC(seurat, c(log10GenesPerUMI = "lower"), log = FALSE)
colSums(seurat@meta.data[grep("^pctMito_", colnames(seurat@meta.data))],
        na.rm = TRUE)
#>   pctMito_3_higher_outliers pctMito_2.5_higher_outliers 
#>                         149                         186 
#>   pctMito_5_higher_outliers 
#>                          45

nmads is in the column name, so nmads = 2.5, 3 and 5 produce separate columns and can be compared side by side. group_by is not in the name, so re-running one metric with different grouping overwrites the previous flags – the summary table is updated to match, so it never describes a column that is no longer there.

log = TRUE is the default and is right for count metrics, which are right-skewed enough that the median and MAD are misleading on the raw scale. Turn it off for anything already roughly symmetric, and for bounded metrics like pctMito whose low end crowds against zero.

Where this leaves you 

seurat <- mergeSeurat(seuratFrom10x(manifest = manifest))
seurat <- diagnoseQC(seurat, organism = "mmu")
seurat <- flagQC(
  seurat,
  metrics  = c(nCount_RNA = "lower", nFeature_RNA = "lower"),
  group_by = "Ident"
)
seurat <- flagQC(seurat, c(pctMito = "higher"), log = FALSE)

getOutlierSummary(seurat)          # what would be cut, and from where
write.csv(getOutlierSummary(seurat), "qc/outlier_summary.csv", row.names = FALSE)

Nothing has been removed at this point. The metrics are on the object, the flags are on the object, and the record of how the thresholds were chosen is on the object. Deciding what to drop is the next step, and it is a judgement call – which is why these functions stop short of making it.
